- The author claims stability of the prepared nanozymes and that the PDI below 0.7 by DLS
indicates good dispersion. However, all the PDI reported are above 0.2 and several above
0.4 indicating highly polydisperse samples for all the PPy-co-PTh nanozymes containing
the different metal ions including the different Ruzymes. Actually, with such a high PDI
there is some risk even in extrapolating the peak maxima by number distribution and z-
potential when using a Malvern instrument…those numbers might not be so solid.
DLS spectra expressed in intensity should also be reported in SI.
- Further TEM measurements should also be provided (more micrographs and higher
quality).
- Figure 2B do not really show “relatively uniform spherical morphology”.
- Potential leaching of metal ions in the relevant biological environments (including in the
presence of iron) should be evaluated.
- ICP-MS and EDS should be performed on all samples and not only on the Ruzyme to allow
for ions-dependent meaningful comparisons of the enzyme-like activities.
- If the activity is supposed to be metal ion type-dependent, considering the polydispersity
index of the samples and the different sizes of nanozymes, a normalization by mass is
not an adequate approach for a meaningful comparison. Especially since it is not clear
from the characterization how many atoms of the different metals are present per
nanoparticles. The current literature suggest that you should normalize the available
active sites and measure the turnover frequency (TOF) to ensure the activity is catalytic
(cycling) (https://doi.org/10.1021/acsnano.1c07520).
- I am afraid that the authors fall into a common analytical mistake. The TMB is not suitable
to be used for pH dependent or temperature dependent studies as performed in this
manuscript (monitoring the absorbance at 652 nm), because the TMB chromogenic
substrate itself is known to be sensitive to the pH variation, leading to remarkable
spectral changes and in addition the TMBox dimer is unstable at neutral pH
(https://doi.org/10.1002/adfm.202315587).
- As a general comment the methodologies reported are not properly detailed and
should be implemented.
- Some of the tests are performed in buffers, including in PBS. The authors should show
that the nanozymes are colloidally stable in these conditions.
- The authors state: “It was observed that Ruzyme significantly increased the O2
concentration in the system and produced more bubbles compared to the other PPy-co-
PTh stabilized nanozymes” It is not clear how the oxygen production was measured. Did
you use an oxygen sensor or this is only based on a naked-eye qualitative assessment?
- The authors should report a full characterization (including TEM and size distribution) of
PVP@Ru and RuO @BSA and all the other nanozymes involved in this study. In the NCT-
NaBH reduction. Considering the strong reducing agent involved how the protein
4
structure will appear after synthesis? Are you sure the NPs structure will resemble to the
one reported in Figure S10A, Ruthenium clusters embedded in unfolded BSA? What kind
of interactions keep them together? I am concerned that the chosen controls are not
appropriate as we know very little about them.
- If the metal ions are supposed to be the active sites during the iron ions scavenging,
is the nanozyme itself, enriched of iron ions, able to perform a Fenton-like reaction? Is
the Iron replacing Ruthenium ions during the scavenging process?
- Structural, compositional, and colloidal stability of the presented nanozymes before
and after exposure to the relevant biological media (cell culture media and mice plasma)
should be assessed.
- In this study the potential role of biomolecular corona on the colloidal stability,
enzymatic-like activity, targeting and internalization/cellular distribution
(https://doi.org/10.1038/s41565-021-00860-0,
https://doi.org/10.1021/acsnano.0c00629,
https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.nanolett.3c01479) should be taken into account. The
amount of proteins present in cell culture medium supplemented with 10% FBS is
sufficient to cover the Ruzyme surface at the concentration used in in vitro experiments?
Ideally, a large excess of protein per NZ’s surface area available should be guaranteed to
mimic the in vivo scenario.
- The author should perform ICP-MS to confirm the uptake of the different Ruzymes and
controls (assessing the metal content per cell) and negative staining TEM to confirm the
mitochondria targeting/lysosomal accumulation (and demonstrating no metal ion
leaching).
- As a general comment the confocal representative images are very dim and the
fluorescent signal is difficult to see on all channels.
- The authors state that the nanozymes are endocytosed. However, the appearence of
ICT-Ruzymes distribution in cells is very different from the one of most of
nanomaterials accumulating in organelles. Why only the uptake of ICT-Ruzyme is
shown and not compared with Ruzymes?
- In general, a comparison between Ruzyme and ICT-Ruzyme is missing: how can the
authors state that the overlap with mitochondria is due to the ICT without this
comparison? In Figures 6F and 6G the results for Ruzyme and ICT-Ruzymes in terms
of ROS and mtROS scavenging are comparable.
- Do the Ruzymes co-localize with lysosomes after 24h incubation as commonly
happens to nanoparticles?
- The efficacy of CICT-Ruzyme in targeting cardiomyocytes in virtue of the CTpeptide
has never been demonstrated in the manuscript, making these data useless, as the
effect of CICT-Ruzyme is very similar to ICT-Ruzyme and Ruzyme (Figure 8 C,D,E,F). A
trend is visible, but is it significant? Eventually, a biodistribution study (via ICP-MS)
should confirm the effectiveness of the specific in vivo targeting.
- Page 19, line 463: “Consistent results were obtained when using O2- ….” Figure S24B
does not show consistent results, and the ROS recovery is not clear from the flow
cytometry spectra. In addition, the data are not presented as an average of n=3, as
stated in the caption.
- Not clear how you exploited here the electrical conductivity of the Ruzyme.

### Reviewer 1

Thank you for addressing my comments in your rebuttal and for the additional data provided. I appreciate the effort to clarify the results. However, several important issues remain, particularly regarding the western blotting and in vivo IHC datasets. To ensure transparency and reproducibility, I ask that the following points be addressed:
1. Western blot data integrity (ACSL4, GPX4, loading controls)
The ACSL4 blots show multiple bands, raising concerns about antibody specificity. A clear, single band at ~80–88 kDa is expected. Please provide uncropped, full-length blots with visible molecular weight markers for all WB data, including loading controls, along with the original raw files. Validation of ACSL4 is required (e.g., knockdown/KO, peptide competition, or a second antibody). I recommend repeating the experiment with a more specific antibody; several validated options are commercially available.
2. Replication and quantification of western blots
Provide quantitative densitometry from ≥3 independent biological replicates, normalized to loading control, with mean ± SEM and appropriate statistical testing. Clarify whether ACSL4/GPX4 panels and loading controls derive from the same membranes (stripped/re-probed) or from separate gels.
3. In vivo IHC (heart sections)
Only one representative image per group is provided in the rebuttal, which is insufficient. Please provide quantified IHC data from >6 animals per group, analyzed across multiple sections per heart, using blinded or automated methods.Provide mean ± SEM with statistical comparisons.
4. Supplementary data and transparency
All uncropped western blot images (with markers, ladders, and all replicates) should be uploaded as supplementary source data. Include a “raw blot index” mapping each cropped panel to its corresponding full-length blot.
Provide raw IHC quantification spreadsheets to support the representative figure conclusion.

### Reviewer 2

The authors have satisfactorily addressed my previous comments. I support the publication of this manuscript after minor revision:
1. In the Method section, the phrase "every MD step" is ambiguous and potentially misleading. The heating procedure from 0 K to 3000 K within 3 ps using velocity scaling typically refers to a continuous temperature ramp during the molecular dynamics simulation, rather than an action performed at each integration step. For clarity, this sentence could be revised as:
"The optimized RuO crystal was heated from 0 K to 3000 K over 3 ps using velocity scaling and equilibrated at 3000 K for
2
0.5 ps via the Nose-Hoover thermostat with a time step of 1 fs to obtain the amorphous RuO structure."
2
2. In the Method section, although many published articles do not explicitly cite resources such as the Materials Project database or the Nosé-Hoover thermostat, I believe it is good scholarly practice to include the appropriate references as a sign of respect to the original sources and to enhance transparency and reproducibility. In this context, the Materials Project can be cited as https://doi.org/10.1063/1.4812323, while the Nosé-Hoover thermostat should be attributed to both
https://doi.org/10.1080/00268970110089108 and https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevA.31.1695.

### Reviewer 3

The authors have undertaken significant additional work, leading to a clear improvement in the scientific level of the manuscript, which is now suitable for publication.
The manuscript show the therapeutic potential of polymer-coated ruthenium based nanozymes engineered to perform protective RONS scavenging to counteract septic cardiomyopathy, showing promising results in vitro and in vivo. Some methodological little detail might still be improved, understandably given the complexity and the size of the work done, nevertheless, the general scientific outcome appear to be solid and impactful, and especially relevant for the Nanomedicine community.

### Reviewer 4

The authors have addressed the raised issues appropriately. I would like to recommend this work to be published.

## Paper

## Abstract

Septic cardiomyopathy (SC) is a severe complication of sepsis that significantly increases patient
mortality. The onset of SC is associated with excessive reactive oxygen species (ROS), leading to
increased oxidative stress and iron accumulation. Herein, we develop a library of conductive
polypyrrole copolymerized polythiophene (PPy-co-PTh)-stabilized nanozymes by coordinating
different metal ions within the copolymer framework. From this library, we identify a ruthenium-
based nanozyme (PPy-co-PTh stabilized Ruzyme) that exhibits significant catalase- and
superoxide dismutase-like activity, as well as nitrogen radical scavenging capability. Modifying
the conductive interface significantly improves the catalytic activity and stability of the Ruzyme
by lowering the catalytic energy barrier, reducing excessive oxidation caused by ROS, and
facilitating the continuous decomposition of ROS. To achieve precise targeted delivery to
myocardial mitochondria, 5-carboxypentyl (triphenyl)phosphonium bromide (TPP-COOH) and a
cardiac-targeting peptide (CTP) are conjugated onto the surface of the PPy-co-PTh stabilized
Ruzyme. In vitro, the stabilized nanozymes effectively scavenge ROS, reduce iron accumulation,
and inhibit iron-dependent cell death, thereby lowering lipid peroxidation. In male SC mice, they
improve cardiac function, demonstrating therapeutic benefits. Given the growing interest in
nanozymes for cardiovascular diseases, this study provides a robust foundation for the
development of therapeutic agents for severe cardiomyopathy and related conditions.

---

## Introduction

Sepsis is a syndrome characterized by a systemic inflammatory response and organ dysfunction
resulting from the body's uncontrolled reaction to infection1. This dysregulated response can lead
to damage to and failure of the heart, kidneys, lungs, and other organs2, 3. Sepsis is one of the
leading causes of death worldwide4. According to statistics, the number of people diagnosed with
sepsis in 2017 was close to 49 million, and the number of related deaths was approximately 11
million, accounting for about 20% of the deaths in that year5. Septic cardiomyopathy (SC) is a
common complication of sepsis2 and presents as an acute but reversible heart disease induced by
sepsis6, 7. SC can resolve within 7-10 days in the early stages, affecting approximately 40% of
sepsis patients8, 9, with an incidence rate ranging from 13.8% to 40%7. The main pathological
features are left and/or right ventricular systolic and diastolic dysfunction10, 11, reduced left
ventricular output12, and decreased ejection fraction (EF)1, 8. Without timely intervention, the
patient’s condition progressively worsens, leading to septic shock, which causes systemic organ
dysfunction and failure. This can result in mortality rates as high as 70%-90%13. Currently, early
clinical diagnosis of SC primarily involves assessing hemodynamics14, electrocardiogram,
echocardiography8, and monitoring afterload-related cardiac function (ACP)11. Certain serum
biomarkers, such as procalcitonin (PCT), C-reactive protein (CRP), and N-terminal forebrain
natriuretic peptide (NT-pro-BNP)11, 15, are also detected to aid in diagnosis. Furthermore, clinical
treatment primarily involves supportive therapies, such as fluid resuscitation and antibiotics, in the
early stages of the disease16; however, targeted interventions are still lacking3. Early diagnosis of
SC, along with a thorough understanding of its pathogenesis and the development of targeted
treatments, is essential for improving patient outcomes and achieving a favorable prognosis.

The pathophysiological mechanism of SC is complex and has not been fully elucidated6. The
contributing factors include systemic cytokine storms (such as IL-1β and TNF-α)17, imbalance of
nitric oxide and reactive oxygen species (R OS)18, endotoxin release8, 19, mitochondrial structural
damage and dysfunction20, high mobility group protein B1 (HMGB1) dysregulation21,
ferroptosis22, calcium overload in cardiomyocytes23, endoplasmic reticulum stress3 and
pyroptosis24. Mitochondria play a central role, as they are the primary site of adenosine
triphosphate (ATP) production. In the adult heart, the ATP needed for cardiac contraction is
produced mainly through mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation and glycolysis, with oxidative
phosphorylation accounting for 95% of ATP generation25. Damage to mitochondria disrupts
oxidative phosphorylation, resulting in excessive free radical production and subsequent
cardiomyocyte apoptosis, as demonstrated in numerous animal studies6, 26. Several clinical studies
have shown that mitochondrial dysfunction can directly contribute to the negative outcomes of
sepsis20. Ferroptosis is a form of regulated cell death (RCD) that depends on iron and ROS22. It
differs from other forms of cell death, such as necrosis, apoptosis, pyroptosis, and autophagy27.
Intracellular iron overload and an abnormal redox system are the main features of ferroptosis28.
Fe2+ accumulates in cells, promotes the production of ROS, and exacerbates oxidative stress and
lipid peroxidation, thereby leading to cell damage29. Iron chelators or lipid peroxidation inhibitors
can prevent the occurrence of ferroptosis30. Iron-mediated cell death has been implicated in the
development of various cardiomyopathies, including SC, cardiac hypertrophy, diabetic
cardiomyopathy, and adriamycin-induced cardiotoxicity22, 27, 31. For example, Shen et al. were the
first to demonstrate the therapeutic potential of melanin nanoparticles as cardioprotective agents,
showing that they alleviate sepsis-induced myocardial injury by scavenging ROS and preventing
iron accumulation, thereby inhibiting ferroptosis32. Wang et al. confirmed that microRNA-130b-
3p (miR-130b-3p) effectively reduces sepsis-induced myocardial injury by inhibiting ferroptosis
in cardiomyocytes10. Thus, previous studies have confirmed that targeting mitochondria and
inhibiting ferroptosis may be effective approaches for alleviating SC.

Oxidative stress is the cornerstone of sepsis pathogenesis, mainly caused by ROS and reactive
nitrogen species (RNS). ROS typically include superoxide anion (O •–), hydrogen peroxide (H O ),
2 2 2
and hydroxyl radical (•OH). RNS mainly include nitric oxide (NO) in free radical form and
peroxynitrite (ONOO–) in nonfree radical form33, 34. Antioxidant therapy is a pharmacological
treatment in which antioxidants help reduce inflammation by scavenging free radicals in the
inflammatory microenvironment35. The body contains various antioxidants, including small
molecules such as reduced glutathione, vitamin A, vitamin E, and trace elements, as well as
enzymatic antioxidants such as catalase (CAT), superoxide dismutase (SOD), and glutathione
peroxidase (GPx)36. Under normal physio logical conditions, small molecule antioxidants and
enzymatic antioxidants work to scavenge reactive oxygen and nitrogen species (RONS),
maintaining redox homeostasis. However, during sepsis, the production of RONS exceeds the
scavenging capacity of these antioxidants, disrupting redox balance. This leads to oxidative stress,
which in turn produces even more RONS, creating a vicious cycle37. It is therefore necessary to
introduce exogenous antioxidants to scavenge excess RONS to mitigate oxidative damage in
tissues and cells.

Nanozymes are nanomaterials with inherent enzymatic properties38. Compared with natural
enzymes, they not only mimic the activity of natural enzymes but also offer advantages such as
lower production costs, greater stability, more diverse functions, and more easily regulated
catalytic activity39. Antioxidant nanozymes may exhibit activities similar to those of SOD, CAT,
or GPx33. Among these, SOD-like nanozymes can convert O •– into H O with relatively low
2 2 2
reactivity, CAT-like nanozymes can catalyze the decomposition of H O into O and H O, and
2 2 2 2
GPx-like nanozymes can decompose H O into H O33, 36. By clearing ROS in the inflammatory
2 2 2
microenvironment, antioxidant nanozymes can help alleviate oxidative stress. Currently, various
nanozymes have been extensively studied in the context of ROS-related diseases, such as the Fe-
Curcumin@Tannin acid (Fe-Cur@TA) nanozyme for targeted myocardial infarction therapy40, the
Prussian blue nanozyme for alleviating Parkinson’s disease41, the Pt-NC single-atom antioxidant
nanozyme for alleviating myocardial ischemia‒reperfusion injury42, and the multifunctional
selenium nanozyme for the treatment of acute lung injury43. However, some nanozymes present
several limitations, including overoxidation, low catalytic specificity, and inadequate stability in
complex physiological environments44. Interfacial modification can effectively enable the precise
regulation of the catalytic activity of nanozymes45. Therefore, a suitably modified interfacial
nanozyme has the potential to represent a clinically applicable category of antioxidants. These
nanozymes can mimic the structure and function of natural enzymes, effectively scavenging
reactive oxygen and nitrogen species (RONS) while restoring redox balance.

In this study, pyrrole and thiophene were used as the frameworks to coordinate various metal
ions, resulting in a conductive polypyrrole copolymerized polythiophene (PPy-co-PTh) stabilized
nanozyme library containing eleven polymers. Following a series of enzymatic activity screenings
and characterizations, a ruthenium-based nanozyme (Ruzyme) was selected for its improved CAT-
like, SOD-like, and nitrogen radical scavenging abilities. To enable precise mitochondrial targeting,
5-carboxypentyl (triphenyl)phosphonium bromide (TPP-COOH) was modified onto the surface of
the Ruzyme, creating the ICT-Ruzyme. Subsequently, ICT-Ruzyme was further modified with a
cardiac-targeting peptide (CTP) to achieve cascade targeting to the myocardial mitochondria,
resulting in CICT-Ruzyme (Fig. 1A). A series of studies revealed that, compared with
nonpolymeric nanozymes (NTCT-Ruzymes), PPy-co-PTh stabilized Ruzymes (Ruzyme, ICT-
Ruzyme, and CICT-Ruzyme) can better prevent themselves from overoxidation in the environment
of excessive H O and have better conductivity and antioxidant properties. Moreover, electrostatic
2 2
forces between conductive polymer nanoparticles can inhibit the aggregation of nanozymes,
thereby enhancing their solubility and dispersion in aqueous solutions. This property allows
nanozymes targeted at the mitochondria and myocardium to disperse uniformly within the heart,
forming an efficient conductive pathway. Additionally, through myocardial and mitochondrial
targeting, PPy-co-PTh stabilized Ruzymes effectively scavenge ROS and chelate Fe2+ in
cardiomyocytes, reducing lipid peroxidation and alleviating oxidative stress, thereby achieving a
precise therapeutic effect on SC (Fig. 1B).

---

## Results

Synthesis and characterization of PPy-co-PTh stabilized nanozymes
Using polyvinyl alcohol, pyrrole, and thiophene as the basic framework, various metal ions were
coordinated to synthesize 11 types of PPy-co-PTh stabilized nanozymes (Fig. S1, Supplementary
Information). A series of structural characterizations were subsequently performed on the 11 types
of PPy-co-PTh stabilized nanozymes. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) confirmed that
the nanozymes exhibited good dispersion (Fig. S2, Supplementary Information). UV‒vis
spectroscopy revealed a distinct absorption peak at 378 nm for all 11 types of PPy-co-PTh
stabilized nanozymes (Fig. S3, Supplementary Information). Dynamic light scattering (DLS) was
used to characterize the PPy-co-PTh stabilized nanozymes. The results showed that their sizes
were predominantly in the range of 50–400 nm, with particle size distribution indices (PDI) all
below 0.7, indicating good dispersion of the nanozyme solutions (Fig. S4, S5, S6, Supplementary
Information). All the PPy-co-PTh stabilized nanozymes showed positive potentials (Fig. S7,
Supplementary Information). Furthermore, as illustrated in Fig. S8, the PPy-co-PTh stabilized
nanozymes containing Fe, Co, Ni, Cu, Mn, Ce, Ru, Rh, Dy, and Pt were found to have an
amorphous structure. However, the PPy-co-PTh stabilized Au-based nanozyme exhibited a distinct
crystalline structure (Fig. S8, Supplementary Information). Overall, a library of 11 polypyrrole
nanobioc catalysts with different metal ion ligands was successfully constructed.

Characterization and screening of the enzyme-like activities of the PPy-co-PTh stabilized
nanozymes
The scavenging of RONS is a key property of nanozymes that enables their antioxidant
mechanisms. The enzyme-like activities of the PPy-co-PTh stabilized nanozymes were
systematically evaluated to identify one with improved antioxidant properties. Peroxidase (POD)
activity catalyzes the decomposition of H O into toxic •OH, and O can be converted to H O by
2 2 2 2 2
accepting electrons under the action of oxidase (OXD) (Fig. 2A). The POD-like and OXD-like
activities of the PPy-co-PTh stabilized nanozymes were evaluated by the 3,3’,5,5’-
tetramethylbenzidine (TMB) probe assay. Almost none of the PPy-co-PTh stabilized nanozymes
produced •OH or H O under the neutral pH conditions typically required for antioxidant effects
2 2
(Fig. 2B-C). Additionally, given the sensitivity of the TMB chromogenic substrate to pH variations,
we further validated the POD-like and OXD-like activities of eleven PPy-co-PTh stabilized
nanozymes at pH 7.4 using o-phenylenediamine (OPD) and 2,2’-azino-bis (3-
ethylbenzothiazoline-6-sulfonic acid) (ABTS) as alternative substrates. The results demonstrated
that, regardless of the substrate (OPD or ABTS), all eleven PPy-co-PTh stabilized nanozymes
exhibited minimal, even negligible, POD-like and OXD-like activities (Fig. S9, Fig. S10,
Supplementary Information).

Nanozymes with CAT-like activity catalyze the decomposition of H O into O and H O (Fig.
2 2 2 2
2D). Since H O has a characteristic absorption peak at 240 nm, the CAT-like activity of the
2 2
nanozymes can be assessed by measuring the decrease in the absorbance of H O at this
2 2
wavelength during the reaction with the nanozymes. Among the 11 types of PPy-co-PTh stabilized
nanozymes, Ruzyme demonstrated the most significant reduction in H O content over time,
2 2
followed by Ptzyme (Fig. 2E). Moreover, O generation during the reaction was monitored to
2
assess the CAT-like activity of nanozymes. Compared with the other PPy-co-PTh stabilized
nanozymes, Ruzyme significantly increased the O concentration in the system and produced more
2
bubbles (Fig. S11, Supplementary Information). These findings indicate that Ruzyme has a strong
ability to catalyze the decomposition of H O into H O and O . Although Ptzyme and Rhzyme
2 2 2 2
simultaneously exhibited CAT-like activity , their catalytic performance was inferior to that of
Ruzyme (Fig. 2E-F; Fig. S11, Supplementary Information).

SOD is an important cellular antioxidant enzyme that can convert O •– to H O 46 (Fig. 2D). The
2 2 2
SOD-like activity of the PPy-co-PTh stabilized nanozymes was assessed using the cytochrome C
assay. In this reaction, O •– interacts with oxidized cytochrome C, generating reduced cytochrome
2
C, which has a specific absorption peak at 550 nm. In the presence of SOD, a portion of O •– is
2
consumed, reducing the absorption of reduced cytochrome C at 550 nm. Thus, the SOD-like
activity of the nanozymes was indirectly evaluated by measuring the inhibition rate. When the
PPy-co-PTh stabilized nanozymes were compared, Ruzyme effectively scavenged O •– even at
2
lower concentrations, with an IC of 0.009368 mg/mL (Fig. 2G; Fig. S12, Supplementary
50
Information).

Both ROS and RNS have the potential to damage DNA in tissue cells, which can subsequently
trigger the development of inflammation47. Therefore, the ability of PPy-co-PTh stabilized
nanozymes to scavenge nitrogen free radicals was examined next, using 2,2’-azino-bis-3-
ethylbenzothiazoline-6-sulfonic acid radical (ABTS•+) and 1,1-diphenyl-2-picrylhydrazine radical
(DPPH•) as substrates (Fig. 2D). The results showed that Ruzyme was relatively more effective at
clearing RNS in a concentration-dependent manner, with its ability to scavenge RNS nearly
matching that of the positive control (vitamin C) (Fig. 2H-I).

Based on a series of enzyme-like activity characterizations of all the PPy-co-PTh stabilized
nanozymes in the library, Ruzyme was selected for its greater ability to scavenge both ROS and
RNS (Fig. 2J-K). Therefore, we chose PPy-co-PTh stabilized Ruzyme for subsequent experimental
studies.

Synthesis and characterization of Ruzyme, ICT-Ruzyme and CICT-Ruzyme
Ruzyme was identified from eleven PPy-co-PTh stabilized nanozymes through high-throughput
screening of enzyme-like activities for further research. ICT-Ruzyme and CICT-Ruzyme were
subsequently synthesized by sequentially modifying the surface of Ruzyme with TPP-COOH and
CTP, as outlined in Fig. 1A. Moreover, nonpolymer nanozymes synthesized using BSA as a ligand
(NCT-Ruzyme) and Ru-nanozymes with the polyvinylpyrrolidone framework (PVP@Ru) were
selected as controls (Fig. S13, Supplementary Information). The EDS mapping diagram displayed
the distributions of Ru, C, N, O, and S elements within the Ruzyme, confirming the presence of
Ru signals in the polymer and providing direct evidence of the successful synthesis of the PPy-co-
PTh stabilized Ruzyme (Fig. S14, S15B, Supplementary Information). The distribution of each
element in the Ruzyme, along with the specific Ru content, was subsequently analyzed via
inductively coupled plasma‒mass spectrometry (ICP‒MS), revealing a Ru content of about 16.42%
(Fig. S15A, Supplementary Information). Additionally, the contents of phosphorus (P) in Ruzyme
and ICT-Ruzyme were detected by ICP‒MS, respectively. The content of P in ICT-Ruzyme was
approximately 0.0057%, but it was not detected in Ruzyme. The addition of P further indicated the
successful ligation of TPP-COOH on the surface of the Ruzyme, and the amount of grafted TPP-
COOH accounted for approximately 0.0844% of the total nanozyme. We subsequently measured
the Fourier transform infrared (FT-IR) spectra of the two nanozymes, ICT-Ruzyme and CICT-
Ruzyme. After CTP modification, distinct stretching vibrations were observed at 1644 and 1343
cm-1 in the spectrum of the CICT-Ruzyme, corresponding to the C=O bonds of CTP, confirming
the successful conjugation of CTP (Fig. S16, Supplementary Information). The Ru contents of the
Ruzyme, ICT-Ruzyme, and CICT-Ruzyme nanozymes detected by ICP-MS were 16.42%, 9.83%,
and 8.69%, respectively (Fig. S17, Supplementary Information). EDS elemental mapping also
revealed the distributions of Ru in the ICT-Ruzyme and CICT-Ruzyme, respectively (Fig. S18,
Supplementary Information). The TEM micrographs demonstrate that the nanoparticles exhibit a
relatively uniform distribution, as illustrated in Fig. 3A and Fig. S19A of the Supplementary
Information. Additionally, the amorphous nature of the nanozyme complex is consistent with the
findings from the high-angle annular dark-field (HAADF) image, which are presented in Fig. S19B
in the Supplementary Information (Fig. S19B, Supplementary Information). Atomic force
microscopy (AFM) measurements demonstrated that the thickness of the Ruzyme was
approximately 6–15 nm, the NCT-Ruzyme had a thickness of about 23–35 nm, and the ICT-
Ruzyme exhibited a thickness of around 20 nm (Fig. 3B-C; Fig. S20, Supplementary Information).
The hydrated particle sizes of the NCT-Ruzyme, Ruzyme, ICT-Ruzyme, and CICT-Ruzyme ranged
from 50 to 100 nm (Fig. 3D). The smaller PDI values of Ruzyme, ICT-Ruzyme, and CICT-Ruzyme
indicated better dispersion of their aqueous solutions than that of the NCT-Ruzyme (Fig. 3E). NCT-
Ruzyme exhibited a negative zeta potential of -34.08 mV, whereas Ruzyme had a zeta potential of
5.272 mV. The presence of lipophilic cations (TPP-COOH) and myocardial targeting peptide (CTP)
in the ICT-Ruzyme and CICT-Ruzyme resulted in increased zeta potentials for both (Fig. 3F). Fig.
3G displays the stability of each nanozyme stored in different biological media (DI water, saline,
PBS, FBS, and DMEM) on days 1 and 7. After 1 mg/mL nanozyme aqueous solutions were
prepared, the NCT-Ruzyme rapidly precipitated in several biological media, whereas the PPy-co-
PTh stabilized Ruzymes maintained better dispersibility over seven days with negligible changes
in particle size (Fig. 3G; Fig. S21, Table S1, Supplementary Information). These results further
indicate that electrostatic forces between conductive polymer nanoparticles can inhibit the
aggregation of nanozymes and that the modification of TPP-COOH and CTP effectively increases
the dispersibility of Ruzyme. X-ray diffraction (XRD) analysis further demonstrated that both
Ruzyme and ICT-Ruzyme exhibit amorphous structures, a finding that aligns with the results
presented in Fig. S19B (Fig. 3H; Fig. S19B, Supplementary Information). Both polypyrrole and
polythiophene are commonly used conductive polymers. Among them, polypyrrole offers
advantages such as easy preparation, high conductivity, stability, and solubility. To assess the
electrical conductivity of the PPy-co-PTh stabilized Ruzyme, electrochemical impedance
spectroscopy (EIS) was conducted, with the nonpolymer NCT-Ruzyme used as a control. The size
of the semicircle diameter in the high-frequency region of the EIS data directly reflects the
electrical impedance of the material, providing insight into the electron transfer dynamics on the
electrode surface. A smaller semicircle diameter indicates lower electron transfer resistance and
better conductivity, whereas a larger diameter suggests higher impedance and poorer conductivity.
As shown in Fig. 3I, compared with the NCT-Ruzyme, the PPy-co-PTh stabilized Ruzyme
exhibited a smaller semicircle diameter in the high-frequency region (Fig. 3I). This indicates that
the PPy-co-PTh stabilized Ruzyme, with polypyrrole and polythiophene as the framework, has a
lower charge transfer resistance. This suggests that the nanozyme facilitates faster charge transfer
during the catalytic reaction, resulting in better electrical conductivity. In conclusion, the
incorporation of polypyrrole and polythiophene effectively enhanced the electrochemical
properties of the nanozyme, linking the electrochemical behavior to the catalytic activity. This
provides support for the subsequent validation of the catalytic performance of the PPy-co-PTh
stabilized Ruzyme.

Characterization of the CAT-like activity of nanozymes and investigation of the mechanism
of H O decomposition

Investigating the mechanism of PPy-co-PTh stabilized Ruzyme to prevent excessive
oxidation and enhance catalytic stability
To investigate the specific mechanisms regulating the activity of the conductive PPy-co-PTh
stabilized Ruzyme, the valence changes of both the PPy-co-PTh stabilized Ruzyme and the BSA-
supported Ruzyme (NCT-Ruzyme) were analyzed before and after the catalytic reaction via X-ray
photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS). XPS analysis of the NCT-Ruzyme and PPy-co-PTh stabilized
Ruzyme before and after the reaction with H O demonstrated that the PPy-co-PTh stabilized
2 2
Ruzyme exhibited greater valence stability under identical catalytic conditions (Fig. 5A-B; Fig.
S26, Supplementary Information). In contrast, the NCT-Ruzyme shows larger shifts, suggesting
greater susceptibility to changes in the valence state. The conductive nature of PPy-co-PTh likely
stabilizes the electronic structure of the Ruzyme, preventing excessive oxidation or reduction. This
stability ensures consistent catalytic activity over multiple cycles, which is crucial for applications
such as RONS removal in sepsis-induced cardiac injury. Density functional theory (DFT)
calculations were performed to elucidate the catalytic mechanisms underlying the SOD- and CAT-
like activities of the NCT-Ruzyme and PPy-co-PTh stabilized Ruzyme. The dynamic equilibrium
structures of the NCT-Ruzyme and PPy-co-PTh stabilized Ruzyme, derived from ab initio
molecular dynamics (AIMD) simulations, were used as the initial models. These structures, which
involve nonpolymer nanozymes and PPy-co-PTh molecules adsorbed on their surfaces, provide
the foundation for investigating the catalytic mechanisms (Fig. 5C). Fig. 5D-G, Fig. S27A-B and
Fig. S28A-B illustrate the proposed mechanisms underlying the SOD- and CAT-like activities of
the NCT-Ruzyme and PPy-co-PTh stabilized Ruzyme. In the SOD pathway, the rate-determining
step for the NCT-Ruzyme is *H O-OOH → *OH + H O , with an energy barrier of 1.465 eV. For
2 2 2
the PPy-co-PTh stabilized Ruzyme, where an electron-conductive polymer is grafted onto the
surface, this energy barrier decreases to 0.702 eV. The rate-determining step then shifts to the final
O desorption step, with an energy barrier of 1.032 eV (Fig. 5D-E; Fig. S27A, S28A
2
Supplementary Information). The catalytic performance significantly improved after grafting with
PPy-co-PTh. In the CAT pathway, the rate-determining step for the NCT-Ruzyme is the final
oxygen desorption, which has an energy barrier of 1.907 eV. For the PPy-co-PTh stabilized
Ruzyme, where an electron-conductive polymer is grafted onto the surface, this energy barrier
decreases to 1.154 eV (Fig. 5F-G; Fig. S27B, S28B, Supplementary Information). This
enhancement is attributed to the PPy-co-PTh modification, which weakens O adsorption and
2
thereby promotes a more efficient catalytic effect. These findings offer important insights into the
molecular mechanisms driving the cascade of SOD- and CAT-like activities in nanozymes, as well
as the mechanisms that contribute to their catalytic stability.

Characterization of nitrogen radical scavenging ability and iron chelation activity of NCT-
Ruzyme, Ruzyme, ICT-Ruzyme, and CICT-Ruzyme
As anticipated, ICT-Ruzyme effectively scavenged oxygen radicals such as O •⁻ and 1O
2 2,
while simultaneously demonstrating robust nitrogen radical scavenging capability, as evidenced by the
reduced amplitude in electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) measurements (Fig. 6A-C). Given
that excessive production of RNS is closely associated with the onset and progression of
inflammation, ABTS•+ and DPPH• assays were conducted to further assess the RNS-scavenging
capabilities of the nanozymes. The results indicated that the nanozymes effectively scavenged
ABTS•+ and DPPH• in a dose-dependent manner (Fig. 6D, F; Fig. S29B-E, S30B-E,
Supplementary Information). The color of the reaction system gradually changed from dark blue
to colorless and from dark purple to yellow (Fig. S29A, S30A, Supplementary Information). The
PPy-co-PTh stabilized Ruzymes exhibited a clearance effect nearly equivalent to that of the
positive control, vitamin C (vit C), as shown more clearly in the full-wavelength scanning image
under identical concentration conditions. NCT-Ruzyme had a less effective clearance effect (Fig.
6E, G). The PPy-co-PTh stabilized Ruzymes demonstrated strong scavenging abilities for both
RNS and ROS.

Iron is a transition metal that readily alternates between Fe2+ and Fe3+ states under certain
conditions. This property gives it a strong pro-oxidative effect, which plays a significant role in its
biological activity29. Studies have shown that excess iron in the body can lead to the accumulation
of highly reactive nontransferrin-bound iron (NTBI) in cardiac tissues. This NTBI forms
intracellular iron pools, which promote the generation and accumulation of RONS, resulting in
mitochondrial dysfunction and lipid peroxidation. Over time, these processes contribute to cellular
damage48, 49. Testing the iron-chelating ability of nanozymes is therefore well justified. The
compound 1,10-phenanthroline reacts with Fe2+ to form an orange‒red complex that exhibits a
characteristic absorption peak at 510 nm. The absorbance of this complex at 510 nm correlates
linearly with Fe2+ concentrations ranging from 0–100 μM, accompanied by a noticeable color
change (Fig. S31A, B, Supplementary Information). This property makes 1,10-phenanthroline an
effective and sensitive indicator for detecting free Fe²⁺ in the system. The results demonstrated that
the PPy-co-PTh stabilized Ruzymes could chelate free Fe2+ in a concentration-dependent manner,
achieving a chelation efficiency of up to 95% at 500 mg/L. The nonpolymer NCT-Ruzyme,
however, exhibited a much lower chelation efficiency of only 30% (Fig. 6H; Fig. S31C-F,
Supplementary Information). This conclusion was more clearly illustrated in the scanning graph
of the system at the same concentration, which demonstrated the strong iron chelation ability of
the nanozymes (Fig. 6I).

Fe2+ can undergo the Fenton-like reaction with H O to generate highly toxic •OH50. Therefore,
2 2
we further investigated whether the iron-enriched nanozyme (PPy-co-PTh stabilized Fezyme,
referred to as Fezyme) itself could initiate the Fenton-like reaction under neutral conditions where
antioxidant activity is typically needed. The results showed that in a pH 7.4 buffer system,
regardless of whether TMB or ABTS was used as the substrate, Fezyme did not exhibit Fenton-
like reaction activity; that is, it failed to effectively catalyze the production of •OH (Fig. S32,
Supplementary Information). This finding indicates that although the nanozyme contains abundant
iron ions, it does not initiate a typical Fenton-like reaction at neutral pH, where antioxidant activity
is typically needed.

After confirming that Ruzyme could effectively chelate Fe2+, we evaluated the potential
leaching risk of metal ions in the relevant biological environment (including the presence of Fe2+).
We simulated the relevant biological environment (PBS buffer) and incubated Ruzyme in iron-
containing (with added Fe2+) and iron-free conditions for 72 hours to perform the ion leaching
experiments. We employed a dialysis method to separate the leached metal ions and used ICP‒MS
for highly sensitive quantitative detection of Ru ions in the dialysate. The results showed that the
relative leaching amount of Ru ions was very low (<0.0002%) in both groups. Although the
leaching rate in the iron-containing group showed a slight increasing trend compared to the iron-
free group (P = 0.0503), the absolute values remained negligible (Fig. S33, Supplementary
Information). This suggests that the risk of Ru ions leaching from the material is negligible,
demonstrating its good stability in biological environments. Moreover, this finding also indicates
from another perspective that the ruthenium sites remain highly stable.

In vitro antioxidant capacity of conducting polymer-stabilized nanozymes
The above results confirm the excellent scavenging properties of PPy-co-PTh stabilized
Ruzymes for ROS and RNS. The safety of the nanozymes was then evaluated using the rat
cardiomyocyte cell line (H9C2) (Fig. S34, Supplementary Information). The results demonstrated
that both polymeric and nonpolymeric nanozymes exhibited good biocompatibility in H9C2 cells,
with minimal cytotoxicity observed at concentrations up to 400 μg/mL (Fig. 7A).

Lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-induced H9C2 cells were used to establish an in vitro model of septic
cardiomyopathy (SC) to evaluate the potential application of PPy-co-PTh stabilized nanozymes
for cardiomyocyte protection in SC (Fig. 7B). The DCFH-DA probe was used to stain
cardiomyocytes treated with nanozymes and/or LPS, and confocal laser scanning microscopy
(CLSM) was employed to observe the intracellular ROS levels. As shown in Fig. 7C, compared
with that in the untreated group, the green fluorescence signal was significantly enhanced
following LPS treatment, indicating that LPS stimulated H9C2 cells to produce and accumulate
ROS. However, after treatment with Ruzyme and ICT-Ruzyme, the green fluorescence intensity
was markedly reduced, suggesting that the nanozymes effectively scavenged intracellular ROS.
However, the NCT-Ruzyme showed no significant effect on the ROS levels (Fig. 7C, Fig. S35,
Supplementary Information). Consistent results were obtained when O •– was used as an inducer
2
to examine the role of nanozymes in scavenging ROS (Fig. S36, Supplementary Information).

Previous results have demonstrated that PPy-co-PTh stabilized Ruzyme exhibits good
biocompatibility and effective ROS scavenging ability. TPP, a commonly used lipophilic cation,
can target mitochondria by enhancing the electrostatic interaction between the delivery vector and
the mitochondria, enabling efficient drug accumulation within the mitochondria51. Mitochondria
are crucial organelles involved in energy production within the cell52. Therefore, to further clarify
the targeting mechanism of the as-prepared nanozyme, we first determined its suborgan
localization in H9C2 cells. However, owing to the low electron density of the polymeric nanozyme,
we were unable to directly observe the accumulation of ICT-Ruzyme in the mitochondria or
lysosomes at the ultrastructural level (Fig. S37, Supplementary Information). Therefore, we further
verified the ability of ICT-Ruzyme to target mitochondria at the cellular level via fluorescence
confocal microscopy. As shown in Fig. 7D, the nuclei labeled with the dye DAPI displayed blue
fluorescence, whereas the nanozymes labeled with the dye Cy5.5 emitted red fluorescence.
Mitochondrial-targeting fluorescent probes, which can penetrate cell membranes, have been used
for specific fluorescence staining of mitochondria in cells53. After 1 hour of coincubation with the
nanozymes, a small amount began to enter the cells. As the coincubation time increased, the red
fluorescence signal gradually intensified, indicating progressive cellular uptake across all systems.
However, different nanozyme systems at the same concentration exhibited distinct uptake
behaviors. Specifically, throughout the incubation period, the fluorescence signal of ICT-Ruzyme
was significantly greater than that of Ruzyme (Fig. 7D). This finding indicates that the
incorporation of (5-carboxypentyl) (triphenyl)phosphonium bromide (TPP-COOH) enables the
nanozyme to target mitochondria, thereby increasing the cellular uptake. To further confirm that
TPP-COOH modification enhances the cellular uptake of ICT-Ruzyme by H9C2 cells, we
compared the ruthenium (Ru) content in cells treated with either Ruzyme or ICT-Ruzyme at
equivalent Ru contents. The ICP–MS results showed that the Ru content in the ICT-Ruzyme group
was approximately 1.2 times higher than that in the Ruzyme group (Fig. 7E). Moreover, TEM
revealed that all the nanozymes maintained mitochondrial structural integrity, demonstrating their
biosafety, which is consistent with the cytotoxicity results from the CCK-8 assay (Fig. S38,
Supplementary Information). Mitochondria are the primary organelles responsible for generating
O •⁻ and inducing cellular oxidative damage, whereas lysosomes serve as the main organelles for
2
phagocytosing exogenous materials54. Therefore, we next investigated the behavior of Ruzyme
and ICT-Ruzyme entry into lysosomes. After H9C2 cells were incubated with the nanozymes for
24 hours, the lysosomes were stained with LysoTracker. The results, as shown in Fig. S39, indicate
that both Ruzyme and ICT-Ruzyme accumulated in the lysosomal compartments, with Pearson’s
correlation coefficients of 0.69 and 0.65, respectively (Fig. S39, Supplementary Information).
In summary, ICT-Ruzyme significantly accumulated in both lysosomes and mitochondria.

Mitochondria are the main site of intracellular ROS production55. Mitochondrial ROS (mtROS)
were detected by staining with the mitochondrial superoxide indicator MitoSOX to assess
oxidative damage. After LPS-induced oxidative damage, a strong red fluorescence signal was
observed in the mitochondria, which decreased following treatment with Ruzyme and ICT-
Ruzyme (Fig. 7F). Quantitative analysis further revealed that both Ruzyme and ICT-Ruzyme
treatments significantly reduced mtROS levels compared to the model group, whereas the NCT-
Ruzyme had no significant effect (Fig. 7G). These results indicate that ICT-Ruzyme effectively
targets the mitochondria of cardiomyocytes, scavenges ROS in the mitochondrial region, and
prevents the generation of intracellular free radicals.

Evaluation of the in vivo biocompatibility of the PPy-co-PTh stabilized Ruzymes
Before studying the use of PPy-co-PTh stabilized Ruzymes for the treatment of SC in mice,
the biocompatibility and biosafety of the CICT-Ruzyme were systematically evaluated in vivo to
assess its clinical translational potential. A total of 20 C57BL/6J mice were randomly assigned to
4 groups: the control group and three CICT-Ruzyme groups (20, 40, and 60 mg/kg). The mice were
then continuously administered the treatments and monitored for 2 weeks (Fig. 8A). The daily
weight changes of each mouse were recorded during the experiment, and no significant behavioral
changes were observed (Fig. 8B). After 2 weeks of treatment, blood biochemical analysis and
complete blood cell analysis were performed. The results showed no significant differences in liver
and kidney function, as well as blood routine parameters, between the control group and the
different doses of CICT-Ruzyme (Fig. 8C-D). These findings indicated that CICT-Ruzyme
exhibited negligible toxicity to the liver, kidneys, and blood of the mice. Similarly, histological
analysis of the major organs of the mice was performed via H&E staining. The results revealed
that CTCT-Ruzyme had no significant histological toxicity, even at the high dose of 60 mg/kg (Fig.
8E). Moreover, the hemolysis test confirmed that the PPy-co-PTh stabilized Ruzymes exhibited
good blood compatibility and did not induce significant hemolysis (Fig. S40, Supplementary
Information). These results indicate that the PPy-co-PTh stabilized Ruzymes possess high
biosafety and biocompatibility.

To subsequently verify the ability of the PPy-co-PTh stabilized Ruzymes to alleviate LPS-
induced cardiac injury, this study first evaluated their cardiac targeting efficacy via in vivo imaging.
For this purpose, Cy5.5-labeled Ruzyme, ICT-Ruzyme, and CICT-Ruzyme nanoparticles were
prepared. Studies have shown that the cardiac-targeting peptide (CTP) with the amino acid
sequence CSTSMLKAC exhibits significant selectivity toward the pathological myocardium56.
Therefore, this experiment was performed using an LPS-induced SC mouse model. Specifically,
SC mice were intravenly injected with equal doses of three types of Cy5.5-labeled nanozyme
dispersions (Cy5.5-Ruzyme, ICT-Ruzyme and CICT-Ruzyme). The average fluorescence intensity
of each nanoenzyme in the organs at different time points (1 h, 3 h, 6 h, and 24 h) was detected via
an in vivo imaging system. Ex vivo fluorescence imaging revealed that the accumulation of
nanoparticles in myocardial tissue increased over time. Moreover, in the SC mouse model,
compared with that in the nontargeted group, the myocardial fluorescence signal in the group
injected with the CTP-targeted peptide-containing nanozyme was the strongest at all time points,
indicating that CTP modification significantly enhanced the targeted accumulation of nanozymes
in the pathological myocardium (Fig. 8F, and Fig. S41, Supplementary Information). To further
validate the targeting efficacy of CTP-modified nanozymes toward pathological myocardium, LPS-
induced SC mice were intravenously administered three types of nanozymes with equivalent Ru
contents. Heart tissues were collected 12 hours post-injection to compare the ruthenium (Ru)
content. The ICP‒MS results demonstrated that the Ru level in the cardiac tissue of the CTP-
targeted peptide nanozyme (CICT-Ruzyme) group was approximately 2.3 times greater than that
in the nontargeted group (ICT-Ruzyme) (Fig. 8G). This result further confirms the ability of CTP
to target pathological myocardium and facilitates subsequent in vivo animal experiments.
Moreover, the accumulation of the three nanozymes in the liver, spleen, lungs, and kidneys was
monitored over time to reflect their metabolic profiles. The results indicated that all three
nanozymes were distributed to varying degrees in each organ, with the most significant
accumulation observed in the liver and kidneys, which is consistent with conventional drug
metabolic pathways (Fig. S42, Supplementary Information).

In vivo therapeutic efficacy of PPy-co-PTh stabilized Ruzymes
Studies have reported that once nanoparticles enter the bloodstream, proteins and other
biomolecules in the blood may interact with them, forming a so-called “biomolecular corona” on
their surface, which alters the intrinsic bioactivity and therapeutic efficacy of the drugs57, 58.
Therefore, prior to conducting in vivo experiments, the PPy-co-PTh stabilized Ruzymes were
incubated with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS) at 37°C for 0, 3, 6, and 18 hours, respectively, to
evaluate the effect of the formed biomolecular corona on the activity of the nanozyme. The
dissolved oxygen content produced by the catalytic decomposition of hydrogen peroxide by
nanozymes after incubation with 10% FBS for varying durations was measured via a dissolved
oxygen meter. The results indicated that as the incubation time with 10% FBS increased, the
biomolecular corona on the surface of the nanoparticles gradually formed, leading to a
corresponding decrease in their CAT-like activity to varying degrees (Fig. S43A-C, Supplementary
Information). This may be attributed to the partial obscuration of the nanozymes’ active sites by
the formed biomolecular corona. Subsequently, their capacity to scavenge reactive nitrogen species
(RNS) was evaluated using ABTS•+ and DPPH• as substrates. The results demonstrated that when
ABTS•+ was used as the detection substrate, the biomolecular corona formed on each nanozyme
after varying incubation periods with 10% FBS had a negligible effect on their ability to scavenge
ABTS•+ radicals. The fact that the color of the reaction system did not change also accurately
confirmed this conclusion (Fig. S44A-E, Supplementary Information). Meanwhile, when DPPH•
was used as the detection substrate, the RNS scavenging capacity of all the nanozymes slightly
decreased with prolonged incubation time, accompanied by varying degrees of color change.
Among them, CICT-Ruzyme exhibited the most significant reduction. Nevertheless, even after 18
hours of coincubation, CICT-Ruzyme retained 60% of its RNS scavenging activity (Fig. S45A-E,
Supplementary Information). We then further evaluated the uptake of ICT-Ruzyme by H9C2 cells
both before and after incubation with 10% FBS. As the coincubation time of the nanozymes with
the cells increased, the red fluorescence signal within the cells tended to increase. However, the
cellular uptake of the nanozyme with a “biomolecular corona” was slightly weaker than that of the
nanozyme without incubation (Fig. S46, Supplementary Information). This finding indicates,
from another perspective, that the “biomolecular corona” formed on the surface of the nanozyme does
indeed affect the efficiency of its cellular uptake. Therefore, PPy-co-PTh stabilized Ruzymes with
a surface biomolecular corona still exhibit considerable ROS and RNS scavenging capacity, as
well as cellular uptake efficiency, which lays a foundation for subsequent validation of the
therapeutic efficacy of these nanozymes in vivo.

To better assess the in vivo therapeutic efficacy of PPy-co-PTh stabilized Ruzymes, an SC
mouse model was established using LPS, and the effect of induction time on cardiac function was
first explored. After intravenous injection of LPS for 12 or 24 h, echocardiography, and histological
examination were performed to evaluate changes in cardiac function and histology, to determine
the optimal induction time (Fig. S47A, Supplementary Information). Cardiac echocardiography
evaluation showed that, compared with the untreated group, a 12-h induction time significantly
altered the cardiac function of the mice, as evidenced by a more pronounced reduction in the left
ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) and left ventricular fractional shortening (LVFS) (Fig. S47B-
D, Supplementary Information). Furthermore, histological analysis revealed more inflammatory
cell infiltration, red blood cell accumulation, and ROS production when the induction time was 12
h (Fig. S47E-F, Supplementary Information). Since SC is reversible within 7–10 days of onset, the
cardiac function of the mice may have entered a compensatory phase after 24 h of induction,
leading to the restoration of cardiac function. Therefore, the induction time of 12 h was ultimately
selected for the subsequent animal experiments.

Next, the SC mouse model was established by intravenously injecting LPS for an induction time
of 12 h. We then used NCT-Ruzyme, Ruzyme, ICT-Ruzyme, and CICT-Ruzyme for treatment (Fig.
9A). According to the results of echocardiography, compared with the control, LPS damaged the
cardiac function of the mice, which significantly reduced the LVEF and LVFS. After PPy-co-PTh
stabilized Ruzymes treatment, the LVEF and LVFS values significantly increased, indicating that
the cardiac function of the mice improved, but the effect of the nonpolymer nanozyme, NCT-
Ruzyme, was not obvious (Fig. 9B-D). In addition, there was no difference in the ratio of heart
weight to body weight among the groups (Fig. S48, Supplementary Information). Serological and
histological assays were then conducted at 12 h to assess the serum concentrations of CK-MB and
LDH, two markers of myocardial injury. The results revealed a significant increase in the serum
levels of these markers in the LPS group compared with those in the control group. However, in
the mice treated with Ruzyme, ICT-Ruzyme, or CICT-Ruzyme, the levels of both myocardial
injury markers were effectively reduced (Fig. 9E-F). As shown in Fig. 9G, histological analysis
demonstrated that, compared with those in the control group, the myocardial tissue of the mice
treated with LPS exhibited noticeable pathological changes. These included infiltration of
inflammatory cells, disordered arrangement of myocardial cells, cell rupture and dissolution,
significantly widened intercellular spaces, and accumulation of red blood cells, indicating
successful induction of myocardial injury by LPS. After treatment with the NCT-Ruzyme, the
intercellular space was restored; however, the infiltration of inflammatory cells and red blood cell
accumulation persisted. However, treatment with the PPy-co-PTh stabilized Ruzymes effectively
improved the tissue structure. The myocardial morphology became clearer, the cells were more
neatly arranged, and pathological damage was markedly reduced (Fig. 9G). As depicted in Fig. 9H,
Fig. S49 and S50, LPS-induced myocardial injury resulted in the generation of ROS, which
increased the level of oxidative stress in myocardial tissue and promoted the apoptosis of
myocardial cells. The CICT-Ruzyme with myocardial targeting ability effectively reduced
oxidative stress levels and the number of apoptotic myocardial cells (Fig. 9H; Fig. S49, S50,
Supplementary Information). Additionally, the RNS scavenging capacity of the PPy-co-PTh
stabilized Ruzymes was verified at the tissue level via the fluorescent probe O52. The results
showed that LPS significantly increased RNS levels in myocardial tissue, whereas treatment with
PPy-co-PTh stabilized Ruzymes effectively reduced RNS levels. In contrast, the NCT-Ruzyme
exhibited no alleviating effect (Fig. S51, Supplementary Information). Subsequently, PVP@Ru,
RuO @BSA, and three previously reported nanozymes were employed as controls to further
2
examine the mitigating effect of the PPy-co-PTh stabilized Ruzyme on SC (Fig. S52A,
Supplementary Information). The results indicated that, compared with the control, LPS
significantly decreased both LVEF and LVFS in mice, leading to a reduction in cardiac function.
Following treatment with nanozymes, cardiac function improved across all groups; however, CTP-
Ruzyme treatment resulted in the most pronounced effects (Fig. S52B-D, Supplementary
Information). PPy-co-PTh stabilized Ruzymes can thus effectively alleviate LPS-induced
myocardial injury and improve cardiac function.

Mechanisms underlying the therapeutic effects of CICT-Ruzyme in alleviating SC
To further investigate the mechanisms through which PPy-co-PTh stabilized Ruzymes alleviate
LPS-induced SC, high-throughput transcriptomics sequencing analysis was conducted on mouse
heart tissues. DESeq2 analysis revealed 2,919 differentially expressed mRNAs between the model
group and the control group, indicating that the SC model was successfully established (Fig. S53,
Supplementary Information). A total of 2,096 mRNAs were differentially expressed following
CICT-Ruzyme treatment compared with the model group, with 1,120 mRNAs upregulated and
1,076 mRNAs downregulated. These findings indicate significant transcriptomic differences
between the model group and the CICT-Ruzyme treatment group (Fig. 10A-C). Gene Ontology
(GO) analysis of the differentially expressed mRNAs indicated that CICT-Ruzyme treatment was
involved in signaling pathways related to the inflammatory response, receptor complex, and
receptor ligand activity (Fig. 10D; Table S3, Supplementary Information). To gain a deeper
understanding of the biological functions and pathways associated with the differentially expressed
genes (DEGs) induced by CICT-Ruzyme, KEGG enrichment analysis was conducted. The top 30
enriched pathways were visualized in a KEGG bubble map. Several pathways, including the
ferroptosis pathway, were identified as being involved in the effects of CICT-Ruzyme treatment
(Fig. 10E).

When the intracellular Fe2+ concentration becomes excessive, the Fenton reaction can generate
a substantial amount of ROS, leading to oxidative stress and lipid peroxidation, which in turn
triggers ferroptosis in cells59. In previous characterization studies, the Fe2+ chelating ability of PPy-
co-PTh stabilized Ruzymes was demonstrated. Building upon these findings, the role of the CICT-
Ruzyme in the ferroptosis pathway was further investigated in cardiomyocytes, guided by previous
characterization and transcriptome analysis results. An iron overload model was established in
vitro using LPS on cardiomyocytes. Iron accumulation in the cells was assessed using FerroOrange,
a fluorescent probe for Fe2+. Excess Fe2+ accumulated in LPS-treated cells, but preincubation with
Ruzyme and ICT-Ruzyme significantly inhibited this process. However, the effect of the
nonpolymer nanozyme, NCT-Ruzyme, was minimal (Fig. 10F; Fig. S54A, Supplementary
Information). Intracellular iron accumulation is a hallmark of ferroptosis, promoting the generation
of ROS and lipid ROS (LOS), which specifically increases oxidative stress within the
inflammatory microenvironment60. To further investigate this, intracellular lipid peroxide (LPO)
levels were measured after incubating the cells with nanozymes and/or LPS using the lipid
peroxidation fluorescent probe (Liperfluo). Coincubation with LPS significantly elevated LPO
accumulation. However, pretreatment with Ruzyme and ICT-Ruzyme led to a significant reduction
in LPO levels, whereas the effect of the NCT-Ruzyme was comparatively weaker (Fig. 10G). The
relative quantitative results were consistent with the above results (Fig. S54B, Supplementary
Information). Prussian blue staining of cardiac tissue showed that iron levels increased in the
myocardial tissue after LPS induction. Treatment with CICT-Ruzyme effectively reduced the
cardiac iron content (Fig. S55, Supplementary Information). These results indicated that the PPy-
co-PTh stabilized Ruzymes effectively reduced ferroptosis-related characteristics, including Fe2+
accumulation and lipid peroxidation, in LPS-induced cardiomyocytes.

RSL3, a GPX4 inhibitor, has been widely used to induce ferroptosis61. Therefore, we employed
RSL3 as an inducer to further validate the inhibitory effect of PPy-co-PTh stabilized Ruzymes on
ferroptosis. We first evaluated the cytotoxicity of RSL3 to H9C2 cells to determine the
concentration that induced approximately 50% cell death, which was identified as 12 μM (Fig.
S56A, Supplementary Information). Subsequently, H9C2 cells were treated with 12 μM RSL3 to
induce ferroptosis in cardiomyocytes, allowing observation of the rescue effects of various
nanozymes (Fig. 10H). The results demonstrated that treatment with PPy-co-PTh stabilized
Ruzymes restored cell viability to over 75%, whereas the NCT-Ruzyme showed no significant
protective effect (Fig. 10I). Liproxstatin-1 (Lip-1), a small molecule that protects cells from death
caused by inactivation of ferroptosis inhibitors62, was used as a positive control. Malondialdehyde
(MDA), an aldehyde produced by the decomposition of lipid peroxides, causes functional
impairment of proteins and DNA in cells and tissues, and serves as a biomarker of lipid oxidation
to evaluate ferroptosis levels63. After confirming the safety of Lip-1 (Fig. S56B, Supplementary
Information), MDA levels were subsequently measured in cells subjected to the various treatments.
As expected, MDA levels were significantly higher in the RSL3-induced cardiomyocytes than in
the control cardiomyocytes. Nanozyme treatment markedly reduced the elevated MDA levels
induced by RSL3, providing evidence that the nanozymes inhibited lipid peroxidation (Fig. 10J).
Ferrostatin-1 (Fer-1), a small-molecule inhibitor that specifically suppresses ferroptosis64. The
cytotoxicity of Fer-1 in H9C2 cardiomyocytes was evaluated, and 2 μM was selected as the
working concentration for subsequent experiments (Fig. S56C, Supplementary Information). The
inhibitory effect of the nanozyme on ferroptosis was subsequently validated by Western blotting.
Acyl-coenzyme A synthetase long-chain family member 4 (ACSL4), a key promoter of ferroptosis,
facilitates the incorporation of free polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs) into cell membranes,
thereby accelerating lipid peroxidation65. Following RSL3 induction, ACSL4 expression increased
in cardiomyocytes. Pre-protection with both ICT-Ruzyme and Fer-1 suppressed ferroptosis, with
Fer-1 exhibiting more pronounced effects than the ICT-Ruzyme (Fig. 10K, Fig. S57,
Supplementary Information). Conversely, glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4), a specific biomarker
associated with ferroptosis, protects cells against lipid peroxidation damage and maintains the
intracellular redox balance66. RSL3 directly inactivates GPX4 through binding, leading to
intracellular lipid peroxide accumulation and ferroptosis initiation61, 66. After treatment with ICT-
Ruzyme or Fer-1, GPX4 expression level was significantly increased (Fig. 10K, Fig. S57,
Supplementary Information). GPX4 enzymatic activity was then measured in drug-treated cells.
The results demonstrated that RSL3 induction significantly reduced GPX4 activity in
cardiomyocytes, whereas both ICT-Ruzyme and Fer-1 effectively ameliorated the RSL3-induced
reduction in GPX4 activity (Fig. 10L). These findings indicate that the ROS-scavenging and
antioxidant properties of nanozymes effectively mitigate lipid peroxidation in RSL3-induced
cardiomyocytes. At the tissue level, GPX4 activity was assessed in LPS-induced myocardial
tissues. Compared with that in the control group, GPX4 activity decreased in the model group but
was effectively restored by PPy-co-PTh stabilized Ruzymes (Fig. 10M). 4-Hydroxy-2-nonenal (4-
HNE), a lipid peroxidation metabolite and critical ferroptosis marker66, 67. The expression and
distribution of 4-HNE in different treatment groups were evaluated by performing microstructural
and quantitative analyses on four discontinuous sections from each cardiac tissue sample. The
results showed that LPS induction effectively elevated 4-HNE expression, whereas treatment with
the PPy‑co‑PTh‑stabilized nanozyme suppressed 4‑HNE levels in multiple cardiac sections,
although the extent of suppression varied among sections and treatment groups, with statistically
significant reductions observed in selected sections (Fig. S58, Supplementary Information).
Collectively, these findings demonstrate that PPy-co-PTh stabilized Ruzymes effectively alleviate
ferroptosis-induced cardiomyocyte damage by significantly inhibiting lipid peroxidation, restoring
GPX4 activity, and modulating key ferroptosis regulators.

Overall, this study further demonstrated the efficacy of conducting polymer-stabilized
nanozymes in alleviating LPS-induced cardiac ferroptosis and lipid peroxidation. The conducting
polymer–stabilized Ruzymes not only exhibit excellent electrical conductivity but also show
enhanced enzyme-like activity and a strong ability to scavenge nitrogen-free radicals, thereby
effectively preventing excessive oxidation and improving nanozyme stability. Their pronounced
antioxidant and iron-chelation properties contribute to the improvement of cardiac function,
highlighting their potential for the treatment of sepsis-related cardiac injury. Moreover, PPy-co-
PTh stabilized Ruzymes exhibit good biocompatibility and safety, providing a solid basis for
potential clinical applications. Beyond the present system, the modification of nanozymes with a
conductive polymer interface offers a general strategy to enhance the catalytic efficiency, stability,
and biocompatibility of conventional nanozymes. This approach may be particularly relevant for
therapeutic applications in diseases associated with electrical conductivity, especially those
affecting the heart and nervous system. Nevertheless, further studies are required to elucidate the
underlying molecular mechanisms and to evaluate the translational potential of these nanozymes
in clinical settings.

Response: We thank the reviewer for their valuable comments. We have carefully read
the suggested reference (https://doi.org/10.1021/acsnano.1c07520) provided by the
reviewer, which states that calculating the catalytic turnover rate (K ) requires
cat
information on the nanozyme concentration.
The key issue lies in how to quantify the active sites. The reference explicitly
mentions: “First, on the one hand, we do not recommend calculating all the metal ions
in the whole NP, since the interior ones are not involved in a catalytic reaction (Figure
6B). On the other hand, considering the entire particle as one enzymatic unit also does
not reflect the true chemical picture (Figure 6A). A more accurate estimation is to
calculate the number of surface sites (Figure 6C).” However, quantifying the exact
number of active sites on nanoparticles remains challenging, but calculating the number
of surface metal atoms can provide a good reference or a reasonable approximation.
This is because “it is unlikely that the number of active sites is more than the number
of surface atoms. Whether each surface metal atom is active or not would require more
detailed surface science and mechanistic studies. But if a catalytic turnover can be
achieved by counting all surface atoms, one can safely conclude the catalysis.” This
necessarily involves morphological parameters.
Specifically, the referenced literature highlights three key morphological parameters:
particle size, crystal facet orientation, and geometric shape. First, the size and shape of
the nanoparticles need to be obtained through electron microscopy. Additionally,
different exposed crystal facets possess different atomic densities. Second, surface area
serves as the foundation for quantifying the number of atoms, and neglecting the
specific surface area can lead to severe deviations in the TON calculation (such as
“Since only 0.32% of the total Fe atoms in the 300 nm NPs are the surface atoms,
considering all the Fe O units as active sites could lead to a drastic underestimation of
3 4
the catalytic turnover”).
The referenced literature indicates that the surface area of nanoparticles can be
calculated via morphological parameters (such as diameter and lattice constant) or via
techniques such as Brunauer‒Emmett–Teller (BET) adsorption. By integrating both the
morphological parameters and specific surface area, this study calculated the TON
values for Fe O NPs, AuNPs (GOx), CeO NPs, and single-atom nanozymes. In
3 4 2
summary, the morphology of nanoparticles (size, crystal facets, porosity) serves as the
fundamental basis for TON calculations, and the specific surface area (determined
through geometric modeling or experimental measurement) is an essential parameter
for quantifying the number of surface atoms. Neglecting morphological factors will
lead to deviations in the TON.
However, in our manuscript, on the basis of TEM observations, our Ruzyme
exhibited an irregular spherical structure. Furthermore, XRD analysis indicates that
Ruzyme is an amorphous polymer without a specific and defined crystal lattice
morphology. Consequently, with the currently available information on Ruzyme, it is
not feasible to calculate the surface active sites of the nanoparticles as described in the
referenced literature.
Additionally, for the nanozymes cited from other literature in our manuscript, we
intended only to perform a longitudinal comparison to demonstrate that the Ruzyme
has a relatively high catalytic rate and superior affinity for H O , revealing its optimal
2 2
CAT-like kinetic characteristics for H O scavenging. Moreover, many of the
2 2
nanomaterials in these references lack the necessary data for such analysis (Table S1),
making it impossible to perform the corresponding calculations.
Accordingly, we will continue to explore more scientific and accurate calculation
methods suitable for determining the active sites of such amorphous nanoparticles. We
once again thank the reviewer for their valuable comments, which provide important
guidance for our future research.

With respect to the impact of NaBH reduction on the structure of BSA during the

formation and stabilization of metal nanoclusters. The evidence in the literature
suggests that proteins such as BSA can maintain structural integrity through specific
metal-coordinating interactions, despite partial unfolding under alkaline or reducing
conditions.
For example, in the study by Xinyue Wang et al.2, during the design and development
of a single-atom nanozyme (BSA-Cu SAN) that highly mimics the natural enzyme
structure based on bovine serum albumin (BSA) with copper (Cu) as the active metal

selected area electron diffraction (SAED) pattern confirmed the amorphous nature of

confirmed the presence of BSA and amide bond. Additionally, molecular docking
simulations (Fig. 1i–j) demonstrated that Cu+ forms stable coordination bonds with
His246/His67 (via N-coordination) and Asp248 (via O-coordination) in BSA.

maintains the “protein-encapsulated nanocluster” structure
(https://doi.org/10.1038/s41392-023-01491-8,

15. If the metal ions are supposed to be the active sites during the iron ions scavenging,
is the nanozyme itself, enriched of iron ions, able to perform a Fenton-like reaction?
Is the Iron replacing Ruthenium ions during the scavenging process?
Response: We thank the reviewer for raising this important question. In response, we
conducted experimental validation focusing on the following two aspects.
First, to evaluate whether the iron-enriched nanozyme (PPy-co-PTh-stabilized
Fezyme, referred to as the Fezyme) would undergo a Fenton-like reaction under
physiologically relevant conditions, we conducted catalytic experiments in a buffer
system at pH 7.4 using TMB and ABTS as characteristic substrates. The results
demonstrated that Fezyme did not exhibit significant Fenton-like activity under these
conditions, indicating that it was unable to effectively catalyze the production of
hydroxyl radicals (•OH). This finding indicates that although the nanozyme contains
abundant iron ions, it does not initiate a typical Fenton-like reaction at neutral pH,
where antioxidant activity is typically needed.
Second, to determine whether iron ions displace ruthenium (Ru) sites during the iron
removal process, we conducted an in-depth investigation through ion leaching
experiments. We simulated the relevant biological environment (PBS buffer) and
incubated Ruzyme in iron-containing (with added Fe2+) and iron-free conditions for 72
hours to perform the ion leaching experiments. We employed a dialysis method to
separate any leached metal ions and used ICP‒MS for highly sensitive quantitative
detection of Ru ions in the dialysate. The results revealed that the relative leaching
amount of Ru ions was extremely low (<0.0002%), with no significant difference
between iron-containing and iron-free conditions, indicating the absence of exchange
or displacement behavior between iron ions and ruthenium ions.
In conclusion, our experiments demonstrate that the iron-rich nanozyme (Fezyme)
itself does not initiate the Fenton-like reaction and that the ruthenium site in the Ruzyme
structure is highly stable and has not been replaced by iron ions.

Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for their important comments regarding the
stability evaluation of nanozymes in biological media. We fully concur on the necessity
of systematically assessing the structural stability, compositional stability, and colloidal
stability of nanozymes in complex biological environments, which is crucial for their
biomedical applications.
With respect to the structural and compositional stability of the nanozyme, we
evaluated the potential leaching risk of metal ions (including the presence of Fe2+) from
the nanozyme in the relevant biological environment. We simulated the relevant
biological environment (PBS buffer) and incubated Ruzyme in iron-containing (with
added Fe2+) and iron-free conditions for 72 hours to perform the ion leaching
experiments. We employed a dialysis method to separate any leached metal ions and
used ICP‒MS for highly sensitive quantitative detection of Ru ions in the dialysate. The
results revealed that the relative leaching amount of Ru ions was extremely low
(<0.0002%), with no significant difference between iron-containing and iron-free
conditions (Figure S33, Supporting Information). This indicates that the risk of Ru ion
leaching from the material is negligible, and the ruthenium sites remain highly stable
without being replaced by iron ions, which effectively demonstrates its excellent
structural and compositional stability in the biological environment.
We also evaluated the changes in the enzymatic activity of the nanozymes after
incubation in biological medium (FBS) for 0, 3, 6, and 18 hours. Although the catalytic
activity decreased to varying degrees with prolonged incubation time, they still
exhibited considerable ROS and RNS scavenging capacity, which functionally
demonstrates the well-preserved structural and compositional integrity.
Furthermore, on the basis of the demonstrated stability of similar polymer-based
nanozymes in biological media, as reported in the literature
(https://doi.org/10.1002/advs.202308251), the polymer nanozymes developed in this
study also exhibit excellent structural and compositional stability. To assess colloidal
stability, we evaluated the stability of the nanozymes stored in different biological

several biological media, whereas the PPy-co-PTh-stabilized Ruzymes maintained

Figure S21, Supporting Information).
